newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai central bank keeps foreign borrowing options.
newsitem.headline: Thai central bank keeps foreign borrowing options.

text.p: Thai central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said on Friday the Thai government would keep open its options of tapping loans from different foreign sources to help it meet a severe liquidity crunch.

Chaiyawat told reporters after holding talks with officials of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on a comprehensive package to revive its battered economy which faces a prospect of growing at its slowest pace in three decades this year.
He declined to say if and how much Thailand would borrow from the IMF and other countries.

"We have sought different options...and held talks with many countries. The Bank of Thailand is working on it. The timing of using them (foreign loans) will depend on its suitability," the central bank governor said.
Chaiyawat declined to comment on market speculation that Thailand may seek a $10 billion standby credit from the IMF to overcome its short-term financial requirement.

The Bank of Thailand has been forced to bail out many private banks and finance companies this year after many of them faced cashflow problems stemming from over-exposure to the troubled property sector.
Chaiyawat and Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya met IMF officials on Friday and their talks on an economic austerity programme is expected to continue over the weekend.
Thanong has said he would seek cabinet approval of the IMF-recommended package next Tuesday.

Jiji news agency reported on Friday that major Japanese banks and banks from other countries are considering extending loans of around $6 billion to Thailand but such assistance would be made available only on condition that the IMF also agrees to provide loans to the country.
Chaiyawat said more remedial long-term measures are required to help revive the Thai economy including those that may affect the majority Thais. He did not elaborate.

Some analysts said the IMF would likely ask Thailand to raise its Value Added Tax VAT) to 10 percent from seven percent, adopt additional government budget cuts, and curb subsidies of state-run utility services.
They said the IMF may also recommend the government to stop using tax payers' money for bailing out private financial institutions.
